# The Week My Van Almost Burned Down, and What I Want Every Groomer to Check on Theirs

On Wednesday, October 28th, at about 2:15 in the afternoon, I was drying a Bernese mountain dog named Moose in a client's driveway in Bedford when I smelled hot plastic.

I figured it was the dryer motor. Dryers get hot, they smell like hot plastic when they're working hard, and I had it on high because Moose is basically a bear and he came in soaked. So I kept going for another minute or so, and then I looked up and saw smoke coming out of the bench seat where my batteries live.

That's the part that's been replaying in my head. Not the smoke itself. The minute before the smoke, where I decided it was fine.

I hit the battery switch. I got Moose out the side door. He was still damp and he thought this was the greatest development of his entire life — open door, new driveway, nobody making him stand still. I used the extinguisher a bit. Honestly I'm not sure I needed to. By the time I got the pin out and pointed it, the switch had already done most of the work. But I didn't know that yet, and when you're standing in a client's driveway watching smoke come out of your livelihood, you don't stand there doing math.

Moose's mom brought me a coffee and sat with me on her front steps while I shook. She didn't try to fix it or tell me it was probably nothing. She just sat there and talked about her neighbour's fence. It was exactly the right thing and I don't think she knows that.

Then I called an electrician.

## First, the boring part where I say what I'm not

I'm a mobile dog groomer. I'm 28, I live in Halifax, and my whole income is a van with a tub in it. I am not an electrician. Nothing in this post is me telling you how to wire your van — I couldn't wire your van and I'm not going to pretend I could.

What I *can* do is tell you what happened, what a real electrician showed me, and the specific things she told me to look at. Priya at Sackville Marine Electric did the actual diagnosis. The numbers below are hers. Where I'm repeating something she said, I've tried to say so, because I don't want anyone reading this and thinking I suddenly know what I'm talking about.

If anything here makes you suspicious about your own build, don't fix it yourself. Get somebody qualified. That's not a disclaimer I'm putting at the top so I can get on with it — it's genuinely the most useful sentence in this whole post.

## What I had

Built in spring 2025 by Coastline Van Fitouts — Darren. The setup:

- 3,000W inverter
- Two 200Ah lithium batteries, 12V
- A 300A ANL fuse
- 4 AWG cable from the battery bank to the inverter

It looked tidy. That's the thing I keep coming back to. The cables were bundled, the runs were straight, everything was labelled, the bench seat closed cleanly over it. If you'd asked me in September whether my electrical was good, I'd have said yeah, it's really clean, the guy clearly cares.

Tidy is not the same as right. Tidy is a cosmetic property. It tells you nothing about whether the copper inside the jacket can carry the load.

## What was actually running through that cable

Here's how Priya walked me through it, in roughly the order she walked me through it, because she's the kind of person who explains things instead of just announcing verdicts.

**The load.** My dryer on high pulls somewhere in the 1,800–2,000W range. The water heater sometimes runs at the same time — I never thought about that, honestly, it's just a switch I flip when I want hot water and I never once considered it as part of a total.

Watts divided by volts gives you amps. At 12V, 2,000W is about 167A before you account for the inverter's own losses — the inverter isn't free, it burns some power turning 12V DC into 120V AC, so call it 10–15% on top. That puts you at roughly 180–190A through that cable just for the dryer. Add the water heater and you're looking at something in the neighbourhood of 240–250A.

Priya's phrasing was that my "normal Tuesday" was already a heavy industrial load by van standards.

**What 4 AWG can take.** Depending on insulation rating and how it's run and bundled, 4 AWG is good for somewhere in the region of 80–100A. Not 250. Not 200. Around 90, give or take, and that's being generous about the installation.

What I should have had, for a 3,000W inverter on a 12V bank, is 2/0. That's a much fatter cable — roughly 280–300A of capacity, which actually covers the load with some headroom.

So the cable in my van was carrying something like two and a half times what it was rated for, every time I dried a big dog.

**Why that turns into smoke.** A wire isn't a perfect pipe. It has resistance, and resistance plus current makes heat. The formula is I²R and the important part is that the current is *squared* — double the current and you quadruple the heat.

Over a run that short, that undersized cable was turning somewhere between 50 and 100 watts of electricity into heat, depending on exactly how long the run was, and doing it inside a closed bench seat with a lid on it. Priya's comparison was a 60-watt lightbulb. Imagine screwing a 60-watt bulb into your battery box, closing the lid, and running it for twenty-five minutes while you dry a Bernese.

And then there's the nasty part: when the voltage sags at the inverter end because the cable can't carry the current, the inverter pulls *more* current to make the same output watts. More current, more heat, lower voltage. It's a loop that only goes one direction. That's why undersized cable doesn't just run a bit warm forever — it holds, and holds, and then one day it doesn't.

**The fuse.** I had a 300A ANL fuse. On its own, 300A isn't a crazy number for a 3,000W inverter — 3,000W at 12V is 250A, so 300A is in the right ballpark for protecting the *inverter*.

But that's not what a fuse is for. A fuse protects the **wire**. The fuse has to blow before the wire is damaged. A 300A fuse sitting on a cable rated for 90A will never blow in time, because the cable fails long before the fuse ever thinks about it. As Priya put it: the wire becomes the fuse. Except the wire doesn't fail cleanly and safely at a known point — it fails somewhere in the middle of a run, under a bench seat, next to a lithium bank.

**The location.** The fuse was mounted about 90cm from the battery positive terminal. Priya works to marine standards, and the ABYC rule is that the fuse goes within about 18cm — roughly seven inches — of the battery. Both those numbers are hers, and 18cm is the conservative marine version.

The reason is that every centimetre between the battery and the fuse is *unprotected*. If a cable chafes through there, or a terminal works loose, or a tool falls across it, there's nothing in the circuit to stop it. And with a lithium bank, "nothing to stop it" means a very large amount of current can move in a very short time. That 90cm — behind a bench seat, in a van that vibrates for a living — was the part of the system nobody had protected at all.

**The fuse type.** Mine was an ANL, which is the common, cheap, everywhere fuse. Priya's spec is a Class T. The difference is interrupting capacity — how big a fault the fuse can safely swallow and still blow the way it's supposed to. The numbers she quoted me were roughly 20,000A for a Class T versus a few thousand for an ANL.

I'm not going to dress that up as something I understand deeply. What I understood from her was: with lithium, if something goes badly wrong, the ANL might not be able to stop it. It might just sit there while the fault keeps going. That is not a coin flip I want to be part of again.

**The crimp.** This one is the one that actually made me feel sick.

A proper crimp is done with a crimping tool — a hydraulic one for cable this size — with the right die, on the right lug for the gauge. A bad one is a lug that was squashed with pliers or hit with a hammer until it looked attached.

Mine was the second kind. Priya knew before she cut anything, but she cut the heat-shrink back to confirm. A bad crimp is a high-resistance joint, and a high-resistance joint is the hottest single point in a whole electrical system. That's why my positive lug was black while the rest of the cable was only melted.

And the heat-shrink is worth talking about on its own. Heat-shrink is good practice. It's also very good at hiding a bad crimp, because it covers the exact place you'd need to look. I'm not saying heat-shrink is bad — it isn't — I'm saying that "it has heat-shrink on it" is not evidence of quality. I took it as evidence of quality. I was wrong.

**The jacket.** The cable's insulation had melted back about 3cm from the lug. That's the number that tells you how close this was. It wasn't smouldering in some inaccessible spot — the actual conductor was hot enough to liquefy its own jacket, and it did that right next to 400Ah of lithium.

## The two things that I keep thinking about

There was no smoke detector in the back of my van. There's the factory one in the cab. That's it. The batteries, the inverter, and the whole rat's nest live in the back, behind me, while I'm facing forward with a dryer in my hand and a dog on the table.

I found out I had a problem because I smelled it. That's not a detection system, that's luck with a nose attached.

The second thing is that Priya showed me her thermal camera shots next to my damage photos. She runs a similar load in her own van — roughly the same inverter, roughly the same size cable run, but built properly. In her shots the cable is a flat, boring colour. Barely above ambient. Mine has a hot spot at the terminal that looks like a cigarette cherry.

Same task. Same load. One of them is a normal Wednesday and one of them is a story I'll be telling for the rest of my life. The difference isn't luck. The difference is a wire gauge and a crimp.

## The checklist

Okay. Here's the part I actually want people to use. This is a visual and physical inspection you can do with the power off — inverter off, battery switch off, and if you can, physically disconnect the battery bank before you start poking around. Priya talked me through all of this and I did most of it on my own van afterwards, in my driveway, with a flashlight, feeling dumb.

**1. Find every cable and read the jacket.** The gauge is usually printed on the insulation — "4 AWG," "2/0," that kind of thing. Write down what feeds your inverter. If you can't find a marking, measure the copper or ask someone who knows.

**2. Measure the run.** Roughly how long is the cable from battery to inverter? Write it down. Longer runs need fatter cable.

**3. Write down your inverter's wattage.** It's on the label. Watts divided by 12, then add 15%. That's roughly the amps going through that cable at full tilt.

**4. Compare.** Now look up an ampacity chart for the gauge you found, or ask a pro to. If your cable's rating is anywhere near your calculated amps — or below it — stop reading and call somebody.

**5. Find your fuse.** Where is it? What's the amp rating? What type is it — ANL, MEGA, MRBF, Class T? How far is it from the positive battery terminal? Measure it. If it's more than a few inches, ask why.

**6. Check whether the fuse could actually protect the cable.** If your fuse is rated for more amps than your cable is, it isn't protecting anything. That's the whole test. You don't need to be an electrician to notice that 300 is a bigger number than 90.

**7. Look hard at every lug.** Grab the cable a few inches back and give it a firm twist and a pull. It should not move inside the lug. Look for green or black corrosion. Look for discoloured heat-shrink right at the terminal — dark brown or black instead of clear. If the heat-shrink is opaque, that can be hiding something. This is the part where I'd honestly just pay someone to look, because it's the part that killed me.

**8. Follow the cable the whole way with your hand and your eyes.** Anywhere it passes through metal, there should be a grommet or a sleeve. Anywhere it's zip-tied to something sharp, that's wear. Vans vibrate constantly and chafe is not theoretical.

**9. Check your battery hold-down.** The batteries shouldn't move. If they can slide, the terminals are moving with them.

**10. Look for household parts.** Wire nuts. Taped splices. Extension cord used as permanent wiring. Speaker wire. If you see any of that in a 12V power run, that's a conversation.

**11. Smoke and CO detector in the back.** Go buy a combo unit. It's thirty dollars. Mount it near the electrical compartment. I did this on day two and I'm still annoyed I hadn't done it before.

**12. Extinguisher.** Know where it is, know it's charged, know the pin comes out easily. Mine was in the van and I still fumbled it. Also — and I'm aware this is rich coming from me — if there's actual fire, get out and call 911 first. I got lucky. Don't take fire advice from a dog groomer.

**13. IR thermometer.** This is the one I'd put on this list even if it was the only thing on it. Forty bucks at Canadian Tire. It's not for the power-off inspection, it's for afterwards.

## The load test, and why the thermometer matters

Here's the thing about electrical problems: a cable with no current through it looks completely fine. You can't see resistance. You can't smell a bad crimp. Everything about my van passed the "looks tidy" test with flying colours, right up until the moment it didn't.

Heat is the tell. So once you've done the power-off checks and nothing's obviously wrong, and you've had a professional look at anything that worried you, here's the gentle version:

Run your normal heaviest load — dryer on high, water heater on, whatever your real Tuesday looks like. Then, *without touching anything*, point the infrared thermometer at the cable, at the terminal where it meets the lug, at the fuse holder, at the inverter terminals. Note the ambient temperature in the van first so you have something to compare to.

Priya's guidance was that a properly built system under load barely warms up. Hers sits close to ambient. If a terminal is running meaningfully hotter than the cable a few inches away from it, or if anything is 15°C or more above the air temperature in the van, that's your signal to stop and get it looked at properly. A hot spot at a terminal is almost always a connection problem, not a cable problem, and it's the cheapest thing in the world to catch early.

Do this with the van ventilated, don't leave it unattended, keep the extinguisher within reach, and don't put your hands anywhere near a live terminal. I'm not going to give you exact pass/fail numbers because I'm not qualified to and the honest answer is that it depends on the install. The point isn't the number, the point is that you now have a way to notice something that was previously invisible.

## If you're about to hire somebody

Tasha. This part is mostly for you, but honestly it's for everyone with a deposit in their hand.

I know you're a week away from paying Darren. I'm not going to tell you what to do — you're a grown adult and it's your money and your van. But here's what I wish I'd asked before I handed mine over, and it's all things a decent builder should be able to answer in a text message without breaking a sweat:

- What gauge cable are you using for the battery-to-inverter run, and what's it rated for?
- What size and type of fuse, and where exactly is it mounted, in inches, from the positive terminal?
- Can I get that in writing, as part of the quote?
- Are the lugs crimped with a proper crimper, and can I see the tool?
- Is the whole system bonded and grounded per the inverter manufacturer's instructions?
- Who does the final inspection, and are they licensed?
- What's the maximum continuous load this system is designed for, in amps?

If someone builds vans for a living, none of that should be a hard question. If asking it gets you a weird vibe, that's information too. A builder who's confident in their work will be happy to write it down, because it protects them as much as you.

Also — and this hurts to type — ask them about their insurance and their warranty in writing. Because if the answer to "what happens if this fails" is "well, it'll be fine," you want to know that before the deposit, not after.

## About Darren

I've gone back and forth about whether to write this part at all.

I'm not trying to wreck anyone's business. I don't think Darren got up in the morning and decided to build a dangerous van. I think he built something that looked right, in a trade where there's no licence required and no inspection at the end and nobody checking your crimps, and it worked for months, and he probably still believes it's fine.

But here are the facts, and people can decide for themselves:

- The build was spring 2025. 4 AWG cable, 300A ANL fuse, fuse about 90cm from the battery, a lug that my electrician says was not properly crimped.
- It failed on October 28th, drying a dog, at a load this system should have handled without any drama.
- As of the day I'm writing this, Darren has not answered three texts and an email. That's four attempts over twelve days.

If he wants to tell his side, my inbox is open and I'll post it. I'm not hiding his name from my own readers and then being surprised when somebody else books him. But I'm also not going to sit here and call him a criminal, because I don't know that and I don't think it's true.

What I'll say is this: the difference between the build I got and the build I should have got is a few hundred dollars in parts. Fatter cable, a Class T fuse and holder, a proper crimp, an extra half hour of labour. That's it. That's the whole gap between a tidy van and a van that nearly burned in a driveway in Bedford.

## Where I'm at

The repair quote is $4,200. That's the main runs rewired in 2/0, a new fuse block, a Class T fuse and holder, and the labour. Three weeks minimum, and some of the parts are on order, so realistically it'll be longer, because that's how parts are.

I've cancelled thirty-one appointments so far. Thirty-one. I've been going through my phone and doing the thing where you apologise eleven times in a text message to somebody whose doodle you were supposed to groom on a Tuesday.

Insurance says maybe. The adjuster is coming Thursday, and I've spent two evenings photographing everything and finding receipts and writing down dates. The electrician's written report is going with it. If you're ever in this position, get the report in writing and take forty photos before anyone touches anything, even though it feels ridiculous while you're doing it.

Rent is due on the 1st. I'm not going to pretend I'm not scared about that. My entire income is that van and right now it's a very expensive box with a melted cable in it, parked where I can see it from my kitchen window. I've been weirdly emotional about the van itself, which surprised me — it's a machine and a tax write-off and a set of shelves, and I've been patting it on the way past like it's a horse.

The dogs are the part that actually gets me. Moose is fine, obviously. Moose is more than fine. But there are thirty-one dogs out there who are going to be very confused and slightly matted for the next month, and their people have been genuinely lovely about it, which somehow makes it worse.

## What happens next

Priya's doing the rewire. I'm using the three weeks to do the things I should have done in spring — new smoke and CO detectors front and back, a proper extinguisher in an actual bracket by the side door, a laminated card in the glovebox with the cable sizes and fuse specs on it, and a printed copy of the whole build spec in the van so that if I ever sell it, the next person doesn't have to guess.

I'm also going to ask Priya to sign off on it in writing. Not because I don't trust her, but because "a qualified person looked at this and here's what they found" is a thing you want to be able to produce at 2pm in a client's driveway.

I'll post an update when the van's back on the road. Probably a photo of Moose looking smug. He's earned it.

And Tasha — ask for the specs in writing. That's all. That's the whole post.

Take care of yourselves, check your cables, buy the forty-dollar thermometer.

— J.

reasons: The piece says Darren's silence has lasted "twelve days", but the request says the fire was "last week"; it also invents that Tasha is "a week away" from paying Darren.
